title: What test-design techniques do you apply to reduce case count while keeping coverage (equivalence partitioning, boundary value analysis, decision tables, state transition testing, pairwise/combinatorial), and how do they help you choose which inputs to test?
shortTitle: Test-design techniques to reduce case count while keeping coverage
topicTitle: What test-design techniques do you apply to reduce case count while keeping cove

s1_definition.profdef: Test-design techniques are systematic methods for selecting a small, high-value set of test cases that covers the important behavior of a system without exhaustively testing every input. Equivalence partitioning groups inputs into classes that the system treats the same, so one representative per class suffices. Boundary value analysis tests the edges of those classes, where bugs cluster. Decision tables enumerate combinations of conditions and their expected actions, exposing rule gaps. State transition testing covers an entity's states and the legal and illegal transitions between them. Pairwise or combinatorial testing covers all pairs of parameter values with far fewer cases than the full cross-product. Together they let a tester justify why a handful of cases gives strong coverage instead of guessing.
s1_definition.analogy: Suppose the National Bank of India accepts transfer amounts from one rupee to one hundred thousand rupees. Testing every single amount is impossible, so a smart tester groups amounts into "too low," "valid," and "too high," and tests one from each group; that is equivalence partitioning. Then the tester checks the exact edges, zero, one, one hundred thousand, one hundred thousand and one, because bugs love boundaries; that is boundary value analysis. When loan approval depends on several yes-or-no conditions like income, credit score, and age, the tester lays out all the combinations in a grid to be sure every rule is covered; that is a decision table. When a loan moves through applied, approved, disbursed, and closed, the tester checks every allowed and forbidden move; that is state transition testing. And when a form has many dropdowns, the tester covers every pair of choices instead of every combination; that is pairwise testing.
s1_definition.oneliner: Equivalence partitioning picks one input per class, boundary value analysis tests the edges, decision tables cover condition combinations, state transition testing covers legal and illegal moves, and pairwise testing covers all value pairs, so you get strong coverage with few cases and can justify every one.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Test-design techniques are systematic methods for selecting a small, high-value set of test cases that covers the important behavior of a system without exhaustively testing every input. Equivalence partitioning groups inputs into classes that the system treats the same, so one representative per class suffices. Boundary value analysis tests the edges of those classes, where bugs cluster. Decision tables enumerate combinations of conditions and their expected actions, exposing rule gaps. State transition testing covers an entity's states and the legal and illegal transitions between them. Pairwise or combinatorial testing covers all pairs of parameter values with far fewer cases than the full cross-product. Together they let a tester justify why a handful of cases gives strong coverage instead of guessing.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Suppose the National Bank of India accepts transfer amounts from one rupee to one hundred thousand rupees. Testing every single amount is impossible, so a smart tester groups amounts into "too low," "valid," and "too high," and tests one from each group; that is equivalence partitioning. Then the tester checks the exact edges, zero, one, one hundred thousand, one hundred thousand and one, because bugs love boundaries; that is boundary value analysis. When loan approval depends on several yes-or-no conditions like income, credit score, and age, the tester lays out all the combinations in a grid to be sure every rule is covered; that is a decision table. When a loan moves through applied, approved, disbursed, and closed, the tester checks every allowed and forbidden move; that is state transition testing. And when a form has many dropdowns, the tester covers every pair of choices instead of every combination; that is pairwise testing.

**One line to remember:** Equivalence partitioning picks one input per class, boundary value analysis tests the edges, decision tables cover condition combinations, state transition testing covers legal and illegal moves, and pairwise testing covers all value pairs, so you get strong coverage with few cases and can justify every one.

sections.s2_technical:
Equivalence partitioning is the foundation. You divide each input into partitions, ranges or categories that the system is expected to treat identically, and then test just one representative value from each partition, because if the code handles one member of a class correctly it almost certainly handles the rest the same way. For a transfer amount valid between one and one hundred thousand, the partitions are below range, in range, and above range, plus invalid types such as negative or non-numeric, giving a handful of cases instead of thousands. The payoff is a dramatic reduction in cases with little loss of coverage, as long as your partitions truly reflect how the system behaves.

Boundary value analysis complements partitioning by attacking the edges, because off-by-one errors and wrong comparison operators cluster exactly at boundaries. For the one-to-one-hundred-thousand range you test zero, one, one hundred thousand, and one hundred thousand and one, and often also the just-inside and just-outside values. Many defects that partitioning alone would miss are caught here, because a bug like using less-than instead of less-than-or-equal only shows at the boundary.

Decision tables handle combinational logic where the output depends on several conditions. You list each condition as a row, enumerate the combinations as columns, and record the expected action for each, which both generates test cases and reveals missing or contradictory rules in the specification. For loan approval depending on sufficient income, acceptable credit score, and minimum age, the table makes explicit what happens for every true-and-false combination, so you neither miss a rule nor duplicate one. You can collapse infeasible or don't-care combinations to keep the table compact.

State transition testing applies when an entity has a lifecycle. You model the states, the events that cause transitions, the legal transitions, and importantly the illegal ones, and you design cases to cover each transition at least once plus attempts at forbidden transitions to confirm they are rejected. For a loan moving applied, approved, disbursed, and closed, you test each valid step and also that you cannot, say, disburse an application that was never approved. Pairwise or combinatorial testing addresses the explosion when many parameters each have several values; testing the full cross-product is infeasible, but most defects are triggered by the interaction of just two parameters, so covering all pairs of values catches the large majority of combination bugs with a small fraction of the cases. Tools generate the minimal pairwise set for you.

The senior nuance is that these techniques are complementary, not alternatives, and choosing inputs is about risk and behavior, not mechanical application. You partition first to shrink the space, apply boundary analysis to the partitions where edges matter, use a decision table where several conditions combine into an action, use state transition testing where an entity has a meaningful lifecycle, and use pairwise where many independent parameters would otherwise explode. The real skill, and what an interviewer listens for, is that you can look at a feature and say which technique fits and why, and then justify your chosen case set as deliberate coverage rather than a random pile of examples.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India transfer accepts amounts from one to one hundred thousand rupees, and testing every amount is impossible. The bank needs a principled way to pick a few amounts that represent all behaviors. This is exactly equivalence partitioning plus boundary value analysis.

Problem 2 — Loan approval depends on three yes-or-no conditions, income, credit score, and age, and the bank must be sure every combination has a defined outcome. This is exactly a decision table.

Problem 3 — A loan has a lifecycle, and some transitions must be forbidden. This is exactly state transition testing.

In the mini-project we build a small library that applies each technique to a banking rule and prints the generated cases, so the demo shows how few cases give strong coverage. We define a `TransferValidator` and `LoanDecision` as the logic under test, and a `TestDesignDemo` that derives partition, boundary, decision-table, and state-transition cases and runs them.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a transfer validator with a one-to-one-hundred-thousand range, a three-condition loan rule, and a loan state machine.

Step 1: Equivalence partitioning runs one representative per class, a negative amount from the invalid class, fifty thousand from the valid class, and two hundred thousand from the above class, covering all three behaviors in three cases instead of thousands.

Step 2: Boundary value analysis runs the edges, zero, one, one hundred thousand, and one hundred thousand and one, catching any off-by-one in the comparison operators.

Step 3: The decision table enumerates all eight true-and-false combinations of income, credit, and age, confirming approval happens only when all three hold and every other combination is rejected, with no rule gap.

Step 4: State transition testing confirms the legal moves applied-to-approved and approved-to-disbursed are allowed, and the illegal move applied-to-disbursed is correctly rejected.

Step 5: The pairwise note shows that three parameters with three values each have twenty-seven full combinations, but roughly nine cases cover all value pairs, catching most interaction bugs with a third of the cases.

sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Feature + its input space
    │
    ├─ many-valued range → EQUIVALENCE PARTITIONING → 1 per class
    │                        │
    │                        └─ edges → BOUNDARY VALUE ANALYSIS (0,1,MAX,MAX+1)
    │
    ├─ several conditions → action → DECISION TABLE (all combos)
    │
    ├─ entity lifecycle → STATE TRANSITION (legal + illegal)
    │
    └─ many params x many values → PAIRWISE (all pairs, not full cross-product)
         │
         ▼
  Small, justified, high-coverage case set
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Test-design techniques are how I get strong coverage from a small, justified set of cases instead of either testing exhaustively, which is impossible, or guessing randomly, which misses bugs. Equivalence partitioning is my starting point: I divide each input into classes the system treats the same and test one representative per class, so a transfer amount valid from one to one hundred thousand collapses to a below-range case, an in-range case, and an above-range case. Boundary value analysis then attacks the edges, zero, one, one hundred thousand, and one hundred thousand and one, because off-by-one errors and wrong comparison operators cluster exactly there and partitioning alone would miss them. Decision tables handle logic where several conditions combine into an action: I list the conditions, enumerate the combinations, and record the expected action, which both generates cases and exposes missing or contradictory rules, which is how I cover a loan approval that depends on income, credit, and age. State transition testing applies when an entity has a lifecycle: I cover each legal transition and also attempt the illegal ones, so I confirm a loan cannot be disbursed without approval. And pairwise or combinatorial testing tames the explosion when many parameters each have several values, because most defects come from the interaction of just two parameters, so covering all value pairs catches the majority of combination bugs with a fraction of the full cross-product.

The key point I make is that these are complementary, not alternatives, and that choosing inputs is about risk and behavior. I partition to shrink the space, apply boundaries where edges matter, use a decision table where conditions combine, use state transition where a lifecycle exists, and use pairwise where parameters would otherwise explode.

At the National Bank of India this discipline paid off directly. For the transfer amount field I replaced a sprawling, ad hoc list of amounts with a tight partition-plus-boundary set and immediately caught a defect where the maximum used less-than instead of less-than-or-equal, so exactly one hundred thousand was wrongly rejected, a bug only the boundary case would reveal. For loan approval I built a decision table that exposed a missing rule for the borderline-age case the spec had not defined. Being able to name each technique, say which feature it fits, and justify my case set as deliberate coverage rather than a random pile of examples is exactly what shows an interviewer I design tests like an engineer rather than writing whatever comes to mind.
